Thank you. I found Q3.4 particularly challenging because using Absalon data feels like a significant invasion of privacy. While it might help identify students earlier, I worry about constant monitoring.

I think Q5.2 is crucial—ensuring the model equally identifies struggling students across groups is essential for fairness.

The group's answers differed most on sensitive data like nationality and financial aid. I lean toward being more restrictive because of privacy concerns, but others see value in improving identification rates. Perhaps an opt-out mechanism could address these differing views? Someone might prioritize accuracy over privacy if they believe the model could significantly improve student outcomes with minimal invasive data.

Thank you for sharing your thoughts.

I found Q3.4 difficult too; while early identification is crucial, using Absalon data feels intrusive and could create unnecessary stress. I also struggled with Q3.5 on sensitive data because balancing privacy and support needs is complex—some data might help but at what cost?

Q4.1 on explainability seems most important for me: understanding why a student is flagged helps build trust and allows for targeted support.

The group’s answers differed most on the use of nationality data. I lean toward "never" because it feels too sensitive, but others see value in improving identification rates. An opt-out mechanism could help address this tension by giving students control over their data.

I think some concerns might be addressed through clearer communication and transparency about how data is used and protected, ensuring students understand the benefits of the model without feeling surveilled.
